overview.text: Search algorithms are procedures that look through data or a possible solution space to find a target, decide it is absent, or identify a best option. For a list, linear (sequential) search checks entries one by one and works even when they are unsorted, but may inspect every entry. Binary search is faster on sorted data: it checks the middle and repeatedly discards the half that cannot contain the target, taking logarithmic rather than linear growth in the worst case. Searching also applies to graphs: pathfinding algorithms explore connections between places, and Dijkstra’s algorithm finds lowest-total-weight routes when edge weights are nonnegative. These methods matter because the chosen procedure affects how much work a computer needs to solve a search task.

key_facts.text: Linear search checks a list from the beginning; if the target is absent, it must inspect all n entries.
Binary search requires sorted data. Each middle-value comparison lets it discard half of the remaining possibilities, so its worst-case work grows logarithmically with list size.
Dijkstra’s algorithm finds lowest-total-weight paths in a directed graph whose edge weights are nonnegative; “shortest” refers to the sum of weights, not necessarily the fewest edges.
Search procedures can report whether an item is present or absent, and the algorithm’s steps can be written as pseudocode before being implemented as code.
